notes.definition: A half equation shows the change at one electrode during electrolysis, including the electrons gained or lost. At the cathode positive ions gain electrons (reduction); at the anode negative ions lose electrons (oxidation).
explanation: Electrolysis is a redox process. At the negative electrode (cathode), positively charged ions gain electrons, so the reactions are reductions. At the positive electrode (anode), negatively charged ions lose electrons, so the reactions are oxidations. The memory aid OIL RIG helps: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

A half equation shows just one of these two changes. Electrons are written as e⁻. For a reduction, electrons appear on the left (they are gained), for example Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. For an oxidation, electrons appear on the right (they are released), for example 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. AQA also accepts oxidation half equations written with electrons subtracted on the left, such as 2Cl⁻ − 2e⁻ → Cl₂.

To write a half equation: first write the ion and the product formed. Next balance the atoms (remember diatomic gases such as H₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and O₂ need two atoms). Then add electrons to the side with more positive charge so the total charge is the same on both sides. Finally check both atoms and charges. For a metal ion, the number of electrons equals the size of the charge: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al.

In aqueous solutions, hydrogen and oxygen can come from water. At the cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. At the anode, when no halide ions are present, hydroxide ions are discharged: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ (or 4OH⁻ − 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O). In molten oxides such as aluminium oxide, oxide ions are discharged: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻.

The number of electrons lost at the anode always equals the number gained at the cathode, because electrons flow round the circuit from the anode to the cathode. This lets you link the amounts of products: when 4 electrons form one O₂ molecule at the anode, the same 4 electrons can form two copper atoms (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu) or two hydrogen molecules at the cathode.
keyFacts: Cathode (−): positive ions gain electrons, which is reduction.
Anode (+): negative ions lose electrons, which is oxidation.
OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.
Reduction half equations have electrons on the left; oxidation half equations have electrons on the right.
Charge must balance on both sides of a half equation.
Metals: the number of electrons equals the ion's charge, for example Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al.
Electrons lost at the anode = electrons gained at the cathode.

workedExamples.title: Writing a reduction half equation
workedExamples.question: Write the half equation for the formation of aluminium at the cathode from Al³⁺ ions.
steps: Atoms already balance (one Al each side).
Charge: left is 3+, right is 0, so add 3 electrons to the left.

workedExamples.title: Writing an oxidation half equation
workedExamples.question: Write the half equation for the formation of bromine at the anode from bromide ions.
steps: Charge: left 2−, right 0, so 2 electrons are released on the right.

workedExamples.title: Linking electrons at the two electrodes
workedExamples.question: Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed. How many copper atoms form for every oxygen molecule produced?
steps: Anode: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻, so each O₂ molecule releases 4 electrons.
Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so each copper atom needs 2 electrons.
workedExamples.answer: 2 copper atoms for each O₂ molecule.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write Cl⁻ → Cl + e⁻ for the anode reaction.
misconceptions.right: In fact chlorine is diatomic, so the product is Cl₂: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often put electrons on the wrong side, such as Cu²⁺ → Cu + 2e⁻.
misconceptions.right: In fact reduction is gain of electrons, so electrons go on the left: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. The charges must balance.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think oxidation happens at the cathode because it is negative.
misconceptions.right: In fact oxidation (loss of electrons) happens at the anode, where negative ions give up electrons.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the number of electrons equals the number of atoms formed.
misconceptions.right: In fact it depends on the charge: one Al³⁺ needs 3 electrons, and one O₂ molecule releases 4 electrons.

realWorld: Engineers use half equations to calculate how much electricity is needed to produce a given mass of aluminium or chlorine.
Electroplating relies on reduction at the cathode, for example Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag to silver-plate cutlery.
Hydrogen fuel cells and rechargeable batteries are described using half equations for the reactions at each electrode.
higherTier: The whole of this subtopic (4.4.3.5) is Higher tier only.
During electrolysis, at the cathode positively charged ions gain electrons, so the reactions are reductions.
At the anode negatively charged ions lose electrons, so the reactions are oxidations.
Reactions at electrodes can be represented by half equations, for example 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ and 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ or 4OH⁻ − 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O.
examTips: Always check that both atoms and charges balance in a half equation.
Reduction at the cathode: electrons on the left. Oxidation at the anode: electrons on the right (or subtracted on the left).
Remember diatomic products: H₂, O₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.
Learn 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ exactly; it is a common exam question.
When asked to identify oxidation or reduction, give the reason in terms of electrons lost or gained.
summary: Half equations show the change at one electrode, including electrons.
Balance atoms first, then use electrons to balance charge.
Electrons lost at the anode equal electrons gained at the cathode.

questions.question: Which half equation is correct for the formation of sodium at the cathode?
questions.explanation: A sodium ion has a 1+ charge, so it gains one electron to become a neutral atom. Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ is the reverse, Na⁺ → Na + e⁻ does not balance charge, and sodium forms positive ions, not Na⁻.

questions.question: Which half equation means the same as 2Br⁻ − 2e⁻ → Br₂?

questions.explanation: Iodide ions lose electrons, so this is oxidation. The other three show ions gaining electrons, which is reduction.

questions.question: Which half equation shows how oxygen forms at the anode during the electrolysis of an aqueous solution?
questions.explanation: Four hydroxide ions lose four electrons, making one O₂ molecule and two water molecules. Check: 4 O and 4 H each side; charge 4− on both sides.

questions.question: Which half equation correctly shows oxide ions being discharged during the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide?
questions.explanation: Two oxide ions (total charge 4−) lose four electrons to form one neutral O₂ molecule. O²⁻ → O₂ + 2e⁻ does not balance oxygen atoms, and electrons are lost, not gained.

questions.question: Why is an equation such as Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu called a half equation?
options: It only shows half the number of atoms
It shows only the reduction (or only the oxidation) part of a redox reaction
It is only correct for half of the electrolysis time
It shows only the reactants of a reaction
markScheme: 1 mark: shows only the reduction or only the oxidation part of the redox reaction
questions.explanation: Electrolysis involves oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode at the same time. Each half equation shows just one of these processes.

questions.question: At which electrode does oxidation happen during electrolysis?
questions.explanation: Negative ions lose electrons at the positive anode, which is oxidation. Reduction happens at the cathode.

questions.question:
Aluminium ions, Al³⁺, are discharged at the cathode during electrolysis.
How many electrons does one Al³⁺ ion gain when it is discharged?
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al. The ion has a 3+ charge, so it needs three electrons to become a neutral atom.

questions.question:
Chloride ions are discharged at the anode during electrolysis to form chlorine, Cl₂.
How many electrons are lost when chloride ions form one molecule of chlorine?
questions.explanation: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Two chloride ions are needed for one Cl₂ molecule, and each loses one electron.

questions.question:
Hydroxide ions are discharged at the anode during the electrolysis of some aqueous solutions.
How many hydroxide ions must be discharged to form one molecule of oxygen, O₂?
questions.explanation: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻. Four hydroxide ions give one O₂ molecule and two water molecules.

questions.question:
Molten aluminium oxide is electrolysed.
Table 1 shows the half equations for the reactions at the electrodes.
3 molecules of oxygen are formed at the anode.
Calculate the total number of electrons released.
questions.explanation: Each O₂ molecule formed releases 4 electrons, so 3 molecules release 3 × 4 = 12 electrons. These 12 electrons reduce 12 ÷ 3 = 4 Al³⁺ ions to aluminium.

questions.question:
Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes.
Table 1 shows the half equations for the reactions at the electrodes.
Calculate the number of copper atoms deposited for every molecule of oxygen produced.
markScheme: 1 mark: one O₂ molecule releases 4 electrons
1 mark: each Cu needs 2 electrons, so 4 ÷ 2 = 2 copper atoms
questions.explanation: Electrons lost at the anode equal electrons gained at the cathode. 4 electrons from one O₂ can reduce two Cu²⁺ ions.

questions.question: Define reduction in terms of electrons.
markScheme: 1 mark: reduction is the gain of electrons
questions.explanation: RIG: Reduction Is Gain. At the cathode, positive ions are reduced by gaining electrons.

questions.question:
Molten potassium chloride is electrolysed.
Write the half equation for the formation of potassium at the cathode.
markScheme: 1 mark: one electron on the left: K⁺ + e⁻ → K
questions.explanation: A K⁺ ion has a 1+ charge, so it gains one electron to become a potassium atom.

questions.question:
Bromine is formed at the anode when molten lead bromide is electrolysed.
Write the half equation for the formation of bromine.
State whether bromide ions are oxidised or reduced.
markScheme: 1 mark: oxidised, because they lose electrons
questions.explanation: Two bromide ions each lose an electron to form one Br₂ molecule. Loss of electrons is oxidation.

questions.question:
Hydrogen gas is produced at the cathode during the electrolysis of some aqueous solutions.
Write the half equation for the formation of hydrogen gas at the cathode.
questions.explanation: Two hydrogen ions each gain one electron, forming one H₂ molecule. Hydrogen is diatomic, so two H⁺ ions are needed.

questions.question:
Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed.
A student wrote this half equation for the reaction at the anode:
Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + e⁻
Explain what is wrong with the student's half equation.
Write the correct half equation.
markScheme: 1 mark: the chlorine atoms do not balance (1 on the left, 2 on the right)
1 mark: the charges do not balance
questions.explanation: Two chloride ions are needed to make one Cl₂ molecule, and each loses one electron, so two electrons are released. Charge: 2− on the left and 2− on the right.

questions.question:
Oxygen is formed at the anode during the electrolysis of some aqueous solutions.
The half equation is:
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
Write this half equation in another way, with the electrons on the left-hand side.
questions.explanation: Subtracting four electrons from the left-hand side shows the same loss of electrons: 4OH⁻ − 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O.

questions.question: At which electrode does reduction take place during electrolysis?
questions.explanation: Positive ions gain electrons at the cathode, which is reduction.

questions.question:
Molten aluminium oxide is electrolysed.
This reaction takes place at one electrode:
2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻
Explain whether this reaction is oxidation or reduction.
Give the electrode at which it occurs.
markScheme: 1 mark: oxidation, because the oxide ions lose electrons
1 mark: at the anode (positive electrode), which attracts the negative oxide ions
questions.explanation: Electrons appear as a product, so they are lost by the oxide ions. Negative ions are attracted to the positive anode.

questions.explanation: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper forms at the cathode; chloride is a halide, so chlorine forms at the anode. Both half equations involve 2 electrons, so the electrons balance.

questions.question:
Sodium chloride solution and copper sulfate solution are each electrolysed using inert electrodes.
Use half equations to explain the products formed at each electrode for both solutions.
Identify which reactions are oxidation and which are reduction.
markScheme: Indicative content: sodium chloride solution contains Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺ and OH⁻ ions; sodium is more reactive than hydrogen so hydrogen forms at the cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (reduction, gain of electrons); chloride ions present so chlorine forms at the anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation, loss of electrons); copper sulfate solution contains Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺ and OH⁻ ions; copper is less reactive than hydrogen so copper forms at the cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction); no halide ions so oxygen forms at the anode: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ (oxidation); reduction at the cathode and oxidation at the anode; electrons lost at the anode equal electrons gained at the cathode.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct products and correct, balanced half equations for all four electrodes, each identified correctly as oxidation or reduction with reasons.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct products for both solutions with at least two correct half equations and some correct identification of oxidation and reduction.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct products or one correct half equation.
questions.explanation: In both solutions, reduction happens at the cathode and oxidation at the anode. The products depend on reactivity (cathode) and whether halide ions are present (anode), and each half equation must balance in atoms and charge.
